title: Capstone: Mini Commerce
subtitle: Build Mini Commerce from design through deployment.
description: Combine Order, Inventory, and Notification. Define contracts, test failures, build a container image, and document how another developer can run and operate the project.

lessons.title: Design & documentation
lessons.summary: Define service boundaries, contracts, and data ownership before implementation.
keyPoints: Keep the initial scope to Order, Inventory, and a Notification worker.
Assign one owner to each data set.
Document failure behavior as well as the happy path.
practice: Draw the order flow and write contracts for POST /orders, POST /reservations, and OrderConfirmed.
Another developer can explain the flow and ownership from the documents.

exercises.prompt: Which capstone scope best demonstrates the concepts within a manageable project?
options: Order and Inventory HTTP services plus a Notification consumer and one complete flow including failures.
Ten services including recommendations and analytics.
One isolated CRUD service with no communication.
Diagrams without running code.
exercises.explanation: A complete flow with failure tests exercises communication, resilience, data ownership, and event delivery without excessive scope.

exercises.prompt: Order the design activities before implementation.
items: Write the main flow from the user’s perspective.
Define service boundaries and data owners.
Write API and event contracts including failures.
Record decisions and trade-offs in ADRs.
exercises.explanation: Business behavior guides boundaries; boundaries determine contracts; ADRs explain the choices.

lessons.title: Build & test failures
lessons.summary: Connect services and storage, secure the APIs, and test timeouts, retries, and duplicate events.
objectives: Implement the order flow with timeouts and idempotency.
Verify behavior during an Inventory outage.
keyPoints: Each documented failure should have a repeatable check.
A failed dependency should produce a bounded response rather than an indefinite wait.
Duplicate events must not create duplicate notifications.
practice: Demonstrate Inventory timeout, idempotent POST retries, consumer deduplication, and local rollback.
Each scenario has a test or reproducible experiment with expected and actual results.

exercises.prompt: Which evidence best demonstrates that Notification is idempotent?
options: An integration test sends the same event ID twice and asserts one notification record.
A code comment saying it is idempotent.
A screenshot of one successful delivery.
90% consumer line coverage.
exercises.explanation: Repeat the event deliberately and assert the resulting side effect count. Comments and coverage alone do not test duplication.

exercises.prompt: When Inventory is stopped, which behavior should Order show according to the previous design?
options: The request completes within its timeout.
The client receives a clear error such as 503 ProblemDetail.
The order succeeds by assuming stock is available.
The request thread waits until Inventory returns.
exercises.explanation: Fail within a defined deadline and report the dependency failure. An open circuit rejects further calls without waiting on Inventory.

lessons.title: Build, release & deploy
lessons.summary: Test first, build an image once, and run that same image with environment-specific configuration.
keyPoints: Promote the same tested image rather than rebuilding per environment.
Use version or commit tags and record the digest.
Application rollback does not reverse database migrations.
practice: Run the same image with local Compose and, optionally, an OpenShift sandbox.
Rollout, health verification, and rollback steps are documented and tested.

items: Run unit and integration tests with ./mvnw verify.
Build the image and tag it with a version or commit.
Push the image to a registry.
Deploy it to staging using staging configuration.
Verify health and run smoke tests.
Deploy the same image to production.
exercises.explanation: Build once after tests pass, then promote the same artifact through environments.

exercises.prompt: How should the application receive a production database password?
options: Inject it from a platform Secret as an environment variable at deploy time.
Store it in application-prod.yml inside the image.
Build a separate production image containing the password.
Pass it as a build argument.
exercises.explanation: Keep secrets out of image layers, build history, and source control. Supply environment-specific secrets at runtime.

lessons.title: Review & handover
lessons.summary: The README should let someone run, test, inspect, and recover the application without relying on your memory.
objectives: Test the README in a clean environment.
Review the project against its definition of done.
keyPoints: Include prerequisites and commands for run, test, deploy, and recovery.
Document unsupported conditions and how to handle them.
Have another person follow the instructions from a clean setup.
practice: Ask another developer to follow the README and record any missing steps.
The project can be run, tested, investigated, and recovered using the documentation.

exercises.prompt: Which sections are essential in the capstone README?
options: Prerequisites and commands to run every service locally.
How to run tests and failure scenarios.
How to inspect health, logs, and traces during a problem.
A complete list of every commit.
exercises.explanation: A useful README explains operation and verification. Git already records commit history.

exercises.prompt: Your outbox relay does not support multiple replicas yet. What should handover include?
options: A known limitation with its impact and a plan to address it.
Hide it so the project looks complete.
Remove the outbox feature.
Ignore it because this is a learning project.
exercises.explanation: State the limitation so the next operator understands which deployment configurations are supported.
